\[
T = (1 - k)\, m + k M + k\, \frac{s}{R}\, (m - M),
\quad
I_{\text{out}} = \begin{cases} 255 & I > T \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases},
\qquad k = 0.5
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(m, s\): The local mean and standard deviation
- \(M\): The smallest value of the image
- \(R\): The largest local standard deviation in the image
- \(k\): The weight of the contrast term

m and s are the mean and the population standard deviation of the window around the pixel. M is the smallest value of the image, and R is the largest s over the image. The same rule can be written T = m - k (1 - s / R) (m - M). Sauvola's rule is T = m - k (1 - s / R) m with a fixed R. So Wolf's method measures from the darkest value M instead of 0, and takes R from the image. Where the window has the highest contrast in the image, s = R and T = m. Where it is flat, T falls from m toward M by the fraction k. This is the rule of Wolf's own program, which uses k = 0.5 by default, and of OpenCV's niBlackThreshold with BINARIZATION_WOLF. If the whole image is flat, R = 0. Then s / R counts as 0 and T equals the value, so every pixel turns 0. The result is 255 where the value is above the threshold and 0 elsewhere, or the reverse with Invert.
